page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.sn1ne.4xlarge is an x86_64 architecture server instance belonging to the ecs.sn1ne family, running on the KVM hypervisor. It is equipped with an Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 processor operating at a clock speed of 2.5 GHz. The instance features 16 dedicated physical cores and 16 vCPUs, resulting in a single thread per core configuration. It is provisioned with 32.0 GB of system memory, yielding a memory-to-core ratio of 2.0 GB per core. The processor features a 35 MB L3 cache and supports AVX and AVX512F instruction sets, though it lacks newer vector extensions like AVX512_VNNI or AMX. This instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, and it provides a baseline network bandwidth of 3 Gbps.

Benchmark data reveals a distinct performance profile characterized by average multi-core capabilities but weak single-core execution. The stress-ng single-core CPU performance falls into the bottom 25%, and the Geekbench single-core score of 930.0 is in the bottom 10%. Single-threaded tasks, such as gzip compression, register poor performance in the bottom 10%. Conversely, multi-threaded benchmarks, including stress-ng multi-core and Geekbench multi-core, achieve average tier results. Memory performance is mixed; while cached small-block read bandwidth is average at 657.15 GB/sec, the overall Passmark memory score is weak, placing in the bottom 25%.

Given its dedicated 16-core compute allocation and 1:2 RAM-to-vCPU ratio, this instance is structured for compute-bound workloads that can leverage multi-threading rather than raw single-core speed. It demonstrates average performance in database operations, static web serving, and software compilation. It is also capable of handling light LLM inference for small models, though performance drops significantly on larger models. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the use of older Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 hardware offers a functional multi-core resource density for legacy workloads, though it presents a tradeoff in single-threaded efficiency compared to newer generation architectures.
